stem: What is the main purpose of departmental accounts?

options.content: To show the gross and net profit earned by each department
options.rationale: Correct: the owner can compare the departments.

options.content: To record the cash received by each department each day
options.rationale: That is the job of the cash book or till records.

options.content: To value the closing inventory of the business
options.rationale: Inventory is counted and valued separately.

options.content: To calculate the tax payable by each department
options.rationale: Tax is assessed on the business as a whole.

explanation: Departmental accounts measure the performance of each department separately.

stem: Which basis is most suitable for apportioning **rent of the shop building** between departments?

options.rationale: Correct: each department pays for the space it uses.
Staff numbers suit shared wages, not building costs.
Revenue suits selling costs such as advertising.
Purchases do not measure use of the building.

explanation: Rent, rates, building insurance and lighting are usually shared by floor area.

stem: Insurance of US\$7,500 is apportioned between the Food and Furniture departments by floor area of 200 m² and 300 m². What is Furniture's share?

options.rationale: This is Food's share.
This shares the insurance equally.
This divides by Food's area instead of the total area.

stem: The wages of a sales assistant who works only in the hardware department are …

options.content: apportioned by the number of staff in each department
options.rationale: Only shared wages are apportioned.

options.content: charged in full to the hardware department
options.rationale: Correct: it is a direct expense of that department.

options.content: shared equally between all the departments
options.rationale: The other departments receive no benefit from this assistant.

options.content: left out of the departmental statement
options.rationale: All expenses appear, either directly or apportioned.

explanation: Direct (departmental) expenses go in full to the department that incurs them.

stem: Advertising of US\$3,600 is apportioned in proportion to revenue. Department X had revenue of US\$45,000 and Department Y US\$27,000. What is Department Y's share?

options.rationale: This is Department X's share.
Correct: revenue ratio 5 : 3, so 3/8 of 3,600.
This uses 3/5 instead of 3/8: the ratio parts were not added.
This shares the advertising equally.

hints: Simplify the revenue ratio, then add its parts.

stem: A department shows a net loss of US\$900 after apportioned rent of US\$3,000. The rent would still be paid if the department closed. What happens to the business's total profit if it closes, assuming no other changes?

options.rationale: This ignores the rent that would still have to be paid.
Rent is not saved, so the loss is not removed.
Correct: the department contributed 3,000 − 900 = 2,100 towards the rent.
The department's contribution of 2,100 would be lost.

explanation: Before rent the department made 2,100. Closing it loses that 2,100 while the rent stays, so total profit falls by 2,100.
hints: Before rent the department made a profit of 3,000 − 900.

stem: In a departmental income statement, the **total** column shows …

options.rationale: Every department is added in.
Revenue, cost of sales and every expense are totalled.
It is a sum, not an average.

options.content: the figures of the business as a whole
options.rationale: Correct: it equals the ordinary income statement.

explanation: The total column adds across each line and gives the business's overall results.

stem: Department A: revenue US\$63,000, gross profit US\$18,900. Department B: revenue US\$36,000, gross profit US\$12,600. Which statement is correct?

options.content: A has the higher gross profit margin: 30% against 35%
options.rationale: A has the larger gross profit in dollars but the lower margin.

options.content: Both departments have the same gross profit margin
options.rationale: The margins are 30% and 35%.

options.content: B has the higher gross profit margin: 35% against 30%
A has the higher margin because its revenue is higher
options.rationale: Revenue size does not decide the margin.

explanation: A: 30%. B: 35%. B earns more gross profit per dollar of sales.
hints: Gross profit margin = gross profit ÷ revenue × 100.

stem: A separate statement of financial position is prepared for each department.
explanation: False. The statement of financial position is prepared for the whole business; departmental accounts split only the income statement.

stem: The sum of the departmental net profits equals the net profit of the business.
explanation: True. Every item is either direct or apportioned, so the columns add up to the total.

stem: Match each shared expense with the most suitable basis of apportionment.
explanation: Building costs by floor area; staff costs by staff numbers; selling costs by revenue; depreciation by the value of equipment in each department.

stem: Electricity of US\$4,200 is shared by floor area: Department P 250 m², Department Q 450 m².

payload.template: Department P's share is US\$ {{blank:a}} and Department Q's share is US\$ {{blank:b}}.

stem: The stationery department had revenue US\$38,500, opening inventory US\$4,200, purchases US\$27,300 and closing inventory US\$5,100. Calculate its gross profit.
Shared wages of US\$22,400 are apportioned by the number of staff: Groceries 4, Clothing 2, Electrical 1. Calculate the share charged to Groceries.
explanation: 7 staff in total: 22,400 ÷ 7 = 3,200 per person; Groceries 4 × 3,200 = 12,800.
workedSolution: 1. 7 staff in total: 22,400 ÷ 7 = 3,200 per person; Groceries 4 × 3,200 = 12,800.

stem: The furniture department's gross profit was US\$14,800. Its share of expenses: wages US\$5,200, rent US\$2,600, advertising US\$1,350. Calculate its net profit.
State **two** decisions that an owner can make using departmental accounts.

points.description: e.g. whether to close / expand a department
e.g. how to share floor space, advertising or staff; whether to change prices or suppliers in a low-margin department; rewarding managers

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Whether to expand the most profitable department or close a weak one, and how to divide floor space and advertising between departments.

stem: Explain why a department with a net loss in the departmental accounts should not automatically be closed.

points.description: Shared (fixed) expenses such as rent and insurance are apportioned and would still be paid after closure
The department may still make a contribution: gross profit greater than the costs that would be saved
Closure could also reduce sales in other departments (customers buy from several departments)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Its loss is after a share of rent and other shared costs that would continue if it closed. If its gross profit is more than its own wages and other avoidable costs, it contributes to those shared costs and closing it would reduce total profit. Customers who come for that department may also buy from the others.

explanation: Compare gross profit lost with costs saved.

stem:
Farai owns a supermarket in Kwekwe with three departments. His departmental income statement for the year ended 31 December 2025 is shown below.

**Farai's Supermarket**

**Departmental income statement**

**for the year ended 31 December 2025**

|  | Groceries US\$ | Butchery US\$ | Bakery US\$ | Total US\$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Revenue | 120,000 | 44,000 | 16,000 | 180,000 |
| Less: Cost of sales |  |  |  |  |
| Opening inventory | 9,900 | 1,250 | 350 | 11,500 |
| Add: Purchases | 92,400 | 30,600 | 9,800 | 132,800 |
|  | 102,300 | 31,850 | 10,150 | 144,300 |
| Less: Closing inventory | (10,800) | (1,400) | (450) | (12,650) |
| Cost of sales | (91,500) | (30,450) | (9,700) | (131,650) |
| **Gross profit** | 28,500 | 13,550 | 6,300 | 48,350 |
| Less: Expenses |  |  |  |  |
| Wages (direct) | 14,400 | 6,300 | 4,600 | 25,300 |
| Rent (floor area 5 : 2 : 1) | 6,500 | 2,600 | 1,300 | 10,400 |
| Electricity (direct meters) | 2,350 | 1,650 | 850 | 4,850 |
| Advertising (revenue) | 2,100 | 770 | 280 | 3,150 |
| Total expenses | (25,350) | (11,320) | (7,030) | (43,700) |
| **Net profit / (loss)** | 3,150 | 2,230 | (730) | 4,650 |

Farai is thinking of closing the Bakery. If he does, the bakery's wages, electricity and advertising will no longer be paid, but the rent of the building will stay the same.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the gross profit margin of the Bakery to one decimal place.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the expenses that would be saved if the Bakery closed.
parts.explanation: Wages 4,600 + electricity 850 + advertising 280 = 5,730. The rent of 1,300 is not saved.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Wages 4,600 + electricity 850 + advertising 280 = 5,730. The rent of 1,300 is not saved.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the total net profit of the supermarket if the Bakery closed (no other changes).
parts.explanation: Gross profit lost 6,300 − costs saved 5,730 = 570. New profit 4,650 − 570 = 4,080.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Gross profit lost 6,300 − costs saved 5,730 = 570. New profit 4,650 − 570 = 4,080.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Advise Farai whether to close the Bakery. Give reasons, and suggest **one** other action he could take.

points.description: Do not close (or a reasoned conclusion consistent with the figures)
The Bakery contributes 570 towards the shared rent / total profit would fall
Bakery products may attract customers who also buy groceries and meat
Other action, e.g. raise bakery prices / cut its wages / reduce its floor space / sell other lines in part of the space

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Farai should keep the Bakery. Its loss is only after a share of rent that will be paid anyway; its gross profit covers its own wages, electricity and advertising and contributes 570 towards the rent, so closing it would reduce total profit to 4,080. Fresh bread also brings customers into the shop. He could improve the bakery's margin by raising prices or reducing waste, or give part of its space to a busier department.

explanation: Closing a department loses its gross profit but saves only its avoidable costs.
hints: Rent is a shared cost that continues after closure.
Effect on profit = gross profit lost − costs saved.
